strings: "2" keeps only ground; "2,9" adds water. To drop tagged noise use mode=remove with "7,18". Classes outside 0-31 are ignored.

50 keeps every 2nd point, 25 every 4th, 10 every 10th. Lower values cut faster but can starve dense-cells below the grid resolution; a tiny minimum is always kept so the stream never empties.

CHM Difference -- Vegetation Height Change (A - B)

Subtracts two CHM mosaics cell by cell to highlight vegetation height change between two surveys or treatments: output = CHM A - CHM B.

Process: Both rasters are aligned to the grid of CHM A; cells where either input is NODATA stay NODATA. The result is a signed raster: positive values mean taller canopy in A, negative values mean taller canopy in B.

Tips: Feed this node with two Input Raster nodes set to the CHM strategy to compare a pre-made CHM against a generated one, or two LiDAR flights (before/after).

Canopy Penetration -- Ground-to-Total Point Ratio

Maps how much LiDAR reaches the ground: for each cell the ratio of ground (class 2) points to all points. Values near 1 mean open ground; values near 0 mean dense canopy blocking the beam.

Process: Ground-classified points are preferred. If the source carries no classification (or no class 2), the map is set to NODATA with a warning instead of producing misleading zeros.

Tips: Raise hole fill distance to close sparse gaps in very dense stands. Lower resolution merges small canopy openings into the surrounding class.

Classify Ground -- Ground Point Classification

Identifies bare-earth points and assigns them to class 2 (ground), writing a classified point-cloud stream for terrain products.

Process: Choose the filtering method with the button on the node (or the Strategy dropdown in the Inspector): PMF (progressive morphology, general purpose), CSF (cloth simulation, noisy or photogrammetric clouds), SMRF (fixed-threshold morphology, flat and agricultural terrain), MCC (curvature plate, dense forest without ground returns) or ATIN (adaptive TIN, stepwise densification from seed minima). Each tile is classified independently and downstream nodes read the shared stream identically.

Tips: Changing the method rebuilds the node's ports and cuts existing connections. Re-runs with another method recompute from scratch (methods never share cached products).

Classify Noise -- Outlier Detection (SOR / ROR)

Flags isolated points that do not belong to a surface:

• Statistical Outlier Removal (SOR) -- points whose mean distance to their k nearest neighbors exceeds the global mean + multiplier x std. Catches isolated high noise (birds, sensor artifacts, multi-return ghosts).
• Radius Outlier Removal (ROR) -- points with fewer than min points inside a radius. Catches sparse low points under the terrain (drop artifacts).

Tips: Run SOR early in the chain (default tag class 18). For low isolated points use ROR and tag class 7. Verify the tagged classes with a color-by-class viewer before removing.

Clip by Polygon -- Area of Interest Mask

Keeps only points inside a WKT polygon (plus an optional outward buffer) and deletes the rest permanently, tile by tile. Boundary points are kept. The polygon is planar XY in the cloud CRS: no reprojection is applied.

Tips: Paste the polygon WKT in the Inspector. An empty polygon blocks the run instead of passing everything (fail-loud beats silent).

Concatenate Tables -- Stack Two Tables

Concatenates two tables (CSV or GeoPackage) into a single CSV with the union of their columns.

Process: Both inputs are read row by row and appended; columns that only exist in one table stay empty in the rows of the other. GeoPackage geometry columns are not exported to the CSV.

Tips: Use this to stack two survey tables into one dataset, or to combine field inventories with plot tables before a downstream analysis.

Consolidate -- Merge One Product Across Segments

Merges the per-segment products of one product type into a single final result, so downstream nodes and the gallery see the consolidated output instead of per-segment ones. Add one instance per product and choose its type below.

Process: Choose the product with the button on the node (or the Strategy dropdown in the Inspector), then connect its provider. The merge waits for all segments and runs in a final session.

Tips: Changing the product rebuilds the node's ports and cuts existing connections.

Decimate -- Point Density Reduction

Prunes every tile to a fraction of its points, keeping the pipeline fast while exploring very dense clouds. Use it when the source LiDAR density is far above what the downstream products need (e.g. grid metrics at 1 m or coarser).

Modes: ratio keeps a fixed percentage of points (default 25%); adaptive targets a fixed number of points per tile instead. When the tile already fits the target nothing is lost (the node is a pass-through).

Strategy: nth keeps every k-th point in file order — fast and deterministic. random keeps the same count as a random sample seeded per tile, avoiding any residual striping in structured clouds.

Tip: the tile cache below this node is untouched, so changing the ratio only reprocesses this node, never the source tiling.

Denormalize Heights -- Restore Absolute Elevation

Inverse of Normalize Heights for clouds that arrive already normalized: adds the wired DTM back (bilinear sampling), restoring absolute elevation so terrain products and merges with unnormalized clouds work again. Points outside DTM coverage or flagged withheld keep their Z and are counted in the payload.

Process: Requires a wired DTM, ideally the same one (same resolution, same surface) used to normalize: another DTM injects a systematic bias, and LAZ quantization alone costs about 1 cm per round trip. The classified stream is NOT re-emitted.

Tips: Denormalize right before terrain products or merges; keep normalized clouds for vegetation analysis.

Elevation Range -- Z Outlier Filter

Keeps points with an elevation inside the configured range, tagging or removing outliers: isolated low points below the terrain and high returns above the survey (noise, birds, cables close to the sensor).

Tips: Set min elevation slightly below the lowest expected ground (drop artifacts sit below the real surface). Adjust max elevation to the tallest legitimate feature (tree tops, buildings). classify (default) is reversible and never deletes ground; use remove only after reviewing the tagged classes.

Export Point Cloud -- Consolidated LAZ

Merges the processed tiles into one point-cloud file. The default export removes tile buffers by keeping only each tile's core area, preventing duplicate points along tile boundaries.

The export can consume the raw, classified, or cleaned stream connected to its input.

File Info -- LiDAR File Inspector

Reads a connected LiDAR source once and writes a structured JSON report: format and header facts, CRS, channels, classifications, flags, flight lines, VLRs, derived densities and QA verdicts.

Process: Single streaming pass over the source file (memory-bounded); one report per connected loader.

Tips: Wire it alone after a loader for a quick survey audit before heavy processing.

Filter by Classification -- Class-Based Finisher

Keeps or removes only the points whose LAS class appears in the comma-separated list. Placed at the end of a cleaning chain it turns the tags produced by Elevation Range / Classify Noise / Scan Angle into actual deletion.

Examples: keep "2" produces a ground-only cloud (class 2); remove "7,18" deletes all tagged noise while preserving every other class. As the tag-to-deletion finisher, this is the step that physically culls points.

Filter by Return -- Keep by Pulse Position

Keeps only the selected returns of each pulse (first/last/single/multiple) and deletes the rest permanently. Single-return pulses are solid surfaces; multiple returns mark porous targets (canopy, wires, fences).

Tips: First returns for surfaces and canopy tops, last returns for ground under vegetation. This node always removes (never tags): review on a sample before chaining deletes.

Flightline Coverage -- Unique Lines Per Cell

Quality-control map of how many flight lines cover each cell. Useful to spot swath edges, drop-outs or overlapping strips in the survey.

Process: Counts distinct point_source_id values per cell (coverage mode) or the point density per cell (density mode). If the source has no point_source_id dimension, the map is NODATA with a warning.

Tips: Cells with a single line are prone to gaps and edge effects; plan extra strips there. Use density mode to check where point density falls below requirements.

Generate CHM -- Canopy Height Model

Computes vegetation height by subtracting DTM from DSM: CHM = DSM - DTM. Only cells where both models have valid data are computed; the rest remain NODATA.

Process: The DTM and DSM mosaics are aligned by their overlapping bounds, then subtracted. Heights are clamped to [min, max] range, and optional Gaussian smoothing reduces noise in the canopy surface. An optional pit-free composite fills small pits for tree work.

Tips: Increase smooth sigma for smoother canopy surfaces in forestry analysis. Lower it for individual tree crown detection. Adjust max height if processing very tall vegetation (e.g. tropical forests with trees over 60m).

Generate DSM -- Digital Surface Model

Creates a surface model capturing the highest return per cell, including buildings, vegetation canopy, and ground.

Process: For each tile, the maximum-Z of all points is rasterized. After merging, holes from sparse coverage are filled by nearest-neighbor interpolation, then optional Gaussian smoothing reduces noise.

Tips: Lower hole fill distance reduces extrapolation artifacts at scan edges. Increase smooth sigma for a cleaner visual surface; decrease for maximum detail in building edges.

Generate DTM -- Digital Terrain Model

Creates a bare-earth elevation model by extracting minimum-Z values from classified ground points (class 2).

Process: For each tile, ground points are rasterized to a min-Z grid. After merging all tiles, optional hole-filling and Gaussian smoothing are applied to produce a clean surface.

Tips: Increase hole fill distance to close gaps in sparse areas. Higher smooth sigma removes micro-topography noise but may flatten real terrain features like small berms or ditches.

Grid Metrics -- Per-Cell Point Cloud Statistics

Computes count, elevation, ground, intensity and noise statistics for every grid cell with points: density planning, quality control and features for downstream nodes.

Process: Core-masked points are binned into global grid cells in one streaming pass; per-tile tables merge exactly by cell key.

Tips: Cells without points produce no rows. Intensity and ground columns are NODATA when the source lacks those dimensions.

Grid Vegetation -- Per-Cell Vegetation Statistics

Computes vegetation structure per grid cell from normalized point heights: percentiles, canopy cover, LAI, VCI, FHD and stratum densities. No CHM needed: heights normalize by the tile ground median.

Process: Vegetation points are binned into global grid cells with 1 m histograms in one streaming pass; tables merge exactly by cell key.

Tips: Percentiles and diversity indices are histogram estimates (1 m bins). Cells without vegetation produce no rows.

Input GeoPackage -- Import an Existing GeoPackage Table

Imports an existing GeoPackage table from disk instead of deriving it from the point cloud, so a table-based pipeline (e.g. joining field inventories with forest metrics) can start from real data.

Process: The selected file is validated (readable SQLite with at least one attribute table) and copied into this run's session, so downstream nodes (e.g. Concatenate Tables) consume it exactly as if it had been generated by the pipeline.

Tips: Use this to bring GeoPackage inventories or auxiliary statistics into a run without pre-processing. Geometry columns are not exported to CSV by Concatenate Tables. Select the file with the Browse button on the node.

Input Raster -- Import an Existing Raster Product

Imports an existing raster (DTM, DSM, CHM or multispectral GeoTIFF) from disk instead of computing it from the point cloud, so a pre-made product can feed terrain or forestry analysis directly.

Process: Choose the product type with the button on the node (or the Strategy dropdown in the Inspector), then pick the file with Browse. The selected file is validated (missing CRS or georeferencing raises a warning) and copied into this run's session as the canonical mosaic, so downstream nodes consume it exactly as if it had been generated by the pipeline.

Tips: Changing the product type rebuilds the node's ports and cuts existing connections. Use this to reuse a product you already have (e.g. a survey-delivered ground model) instead of processing the LiDAR from scratch.

Input Table -- Import an Existing Table

Imports an existing CSV table from disk instead of deriving it from the point cloud, so a table-based pipeline (e.g. joining ascii inventories with forest metrics) can start from real data.

Process: The selected file is validated (readable header + rows) and copied into this run's session, so downstream nodes (e.g. Concatenate Tables) consume it exactly as if it had been generated by the pipeline.

Tips: Use this to bring plot inventories, field tables or auxiliary statistics into a run without pre-processing. Select the file with the Browse button on the node.

Intensity Orthophoto -- Mean LiDAR Intensity Per Cell

Renders the average return intensity as an ortho-like raster, useful as an optical proxy for timber volume, species contrast or surface differences across the survey.

Process: Per cell, the mean intensity of the returns is computed and optionally NODATA-aware median filtered. Scan-angle normalization (I / cos(theta)) compensates the darker edges of each swath; points beyond max scan angle are discarded.

Tips: Keep normalize scan angle on to avoid dark strip edges. Raise the max scan angle only if data is sparse near the swath borders.

Intensity Range -- Return Strength Filter

Keeps points whose intensity (returned signal strength) falls inside the configured range. Extremely weak returns are usually atmospheric noise or edge hits with unreliable geometry; saturated returns may bias metrics on reflective surfaces.

Tips: Inspect the intensity histogram first (Intensity Ortho viewer) and set the bounds slightly inside the real signal peak. Over-aggressive filtering of low intensity can remove real returns from dark or wet surfaces. classify (default) keeps the cloud intact.

Load LAS/LAZ -- Point Cloud Source

Loads a LAS/LAZ file and advertises the point cloud to the pipeline. The file is tiled automatically so downstream nodes can process it in parallel parts.

Process: The file is read in chunks and divided into spatial tiles. A buffer margin is added around each tile so that features crossing tile boundaries are fully contained in at least one tile. Downstream nodes consume the point cloud in these per-tile parts.

Tiling: The Tiling group controls the tile size, buffer and per-tile point cap of the source pass. The Segmentation group runs the pipeline in sequential batches over groups of whole tiles, bounding the memory envelope of each pass (0 = one single pass).

Normalize Heights -- Height Above Ground

Replaces Z with height above the wired DTM (bilinear sampling, exact on slopes): vegetation and buildings read as height over ground. Points outside DTM coverage or flagged withheld keep their original Z and are counted in the payload.

Process: Requires a wired DTM. The classified stream is NOT re-emitted: downstream terrain products must use the pre-normalize stream, or they will surface heights as elevation.

Tips: Normalize right before vegetation analysis; keep the classified stream for terrain.

Scan Angle -- Off-Nadir Return Filter

Keeps points acquired within the configured scan angle range (degrees from nadir). Wide-angle returns have stretched footprints, weaker intensity and worse vertical precision, so trimming the extremes improves ground classification and surface quality.

Tips: Typical airborne LiDAR keeps angles within +/-25 to +/-40 degrees. The dimension is auto-detected as scan_angle (LAS 1.4) or scan_angle_rank (older formats). If the source has no scan angle dimension the node passes points through and warns.

Terrain Derivatives -- Slope, Aspect and Hillshade from a DTM

Derives terrain surfaces from a wired DTM mosaic with Horn (1981) 3x3 operators: slope in degrees, aspect clockwise from north (flat cells read -1), and hillshade 0-255 for the configured sun.

Process: Choose the derivative with the button on the node (or the Strategy dropdown in the Inspector). Cells whose 3x3 window touches NODATA stay NODATA, and a 1-cell rim stays NODATA by design.

Tips: Feed it a DTM (bare earth). Slope honors z_factor for vertical exaggeration; the hillshade sun defaults to the 315/45 cartographic standard.

Vegetation Index -- Crop Vigor from Multispectral Bands

Computes a normalized difference vegetation index cell by cell from two bands of a multispectral orthomosaic: index = (A - B) / (A + B) in [-1, 1].

Process: Pick the preset (NDVI, NDRE, GNDVI, SAVI) or Custom (which reuses the red/NIR band pair) and the 1-based band numbers of your sensor. Cells where either band is NODATA (or the denominator is zero) stay NODATA.

Tips: Feed this node with an Input Raster node set to the Multispectral strategy. Check your sensor band order first (defaults follow the common Blue/Green/Red/RedEdge/NIR layout). Check band count first: a single-band file is a finished product, not a multispectral source. RGB-only indices (VARI, GLI) are illumination-sensitive proxies, not a replacement for NIR-based ones.

max gives the standard canopy surface DSM. mean smooths the surface. median is robust to outliers. idw (Inverse Distance Weighted) interpolates between points for denser coverage.

min gives the standard bare-earth DTM. mean smooths the surface but may overestimate ground under sparse canopy. median is robust to outliers. idw (Inverse Distance Weighted) interpolates between points for denser coverage.

nth keeps every k-th point in file order: fastest and fully deterministic, ideal for huge files. random keeps the same count but picks a different (still deterministic) subset per tile, removing potential striping in regularly structured clouds.

ratio is the simplest way to thin a dense cloud (start at 25%). adaptive is more predictable across heterogeneous data: it keeps roughly the requested point count per tile regardless of its original density.
sor (Statistical Outlier Removal) flags isolated high noise using neighborhood distances. ror (Radius Outlier Removal) flags isolated low points too sparse to belong to a surface.
